Sacred revelations orally transmitted by brahmins from generation to generation, differing from traditional law codes (smrithi). Divinely sourced scripture; Veda; divine words known by revelation; that which was heard or listened to.
A sage, the son of Bharadwaja.
One part of the Yajur-veda, the White Yajur-veda, promoted by Yajnavalkya.
The sun god, the father of time. A name for the sun. Also, son of Kasyapa and father of Manu.
Nerve current passing through the spinal column from the basal plexus (muladhara) to the crown of the head (sahasrara).
Form, essential nature, true nature of Being, embodiment.
A great sage; the first person to argue aginst the evils of drinking and adultery by the brahmins; son of Uddalaka.

Entity associated with dream state composed of mind, intellect, five vital airs, five senses of perception, and the five elements; the experiencer of the dream or subconscious state, “light” of the subconscious.
One of the ten most important Upanishads; it is the philosophical portion of the Black Yajur-veda; the other part is called the White Yajur-veda.
Concentrated spiritual exercises to attain God, penance, severe austerities.
Philosophical system based on reasoning or logic.
One of the gunas (qualities and dispositions) of maya or prakriti. It is the quality of dullness, inertia, darkness and tendency to evil. It results in ignorance.
Adjective form of thamas, dull, ignorant, passive.
Quality of dullness, ignorance, delusion, inactivity, inertia, sloth. Associated with colour black. See guna.
Principle, truth, essence. That-this entity. Thathwa is regarded as made up of That (Thath) and you (thwam).
You are That. One of four great Vedantic statements expressing the non-difference of individual soul and Brahman, the supreme absolute Self.
A lunar day; the moon increases for 15 thithis and decreases for 15.
The second in the cycle of four eras. See yuga.
“Beyond” stage in samadhi; fourth stage beyond waking, dream, and deep sleep. Superconscious state.
Breath that moves upward from the throat.
Teaching; advice; initiation; communication of an initiatory mantra or formula.
Sacred thread ceremony in which a boy is initiated with a sacred thread and is then qualified to learn Vedas.

The very sacred portions of the Vedas that deal with God, humanity, and universe, their nature and interrelationships. Spiritual knowledge (jnana) is their content, so they form the Jnana-kanda of the Vedas Principle message is nondualism: unity of Brahman and Atma.
Worship, devotion, meditation practice, acquisition of the presence of the Lord, a method for approaching or getting close to a deity or God, the act of being near or at hand.
Vocal organs, word, word of mouth.
A disciple of Pippalada, born in the line of Bhrigu. Also named Bhargava.
Omnipresent, Supreme Self. Name for Sun; means “sum total of created beings”.
Section of the Vedas taught by the Sun in the form of a horse (vaji).
The saint-poet who wrote the Ramayana.
Ancient hermit. Friend of Vasishta and a priest of Dasaratha; he composed Rig-vedic hymns.
Inclination, impression of anything remaining in the subconscious mind from past action.
Chief Rig-vedic god associated with Mitra; god of rain, water, the ocean, night; a great sage.
One of the greatest rishis (sages) of ancient times; priest of the solar race of kings; revealer of several Vedic hymns. Had sacred, wishfulfilling cow called Nandini.
Subsidiary treatises of the Vedas: Six sciences of proper pronunciation, grammar, metre, etymology, astronomy, ritual.

Means “the end of the Vedas”. It is the essence of the Vedas enshrined in the Upanishads. The philosophy of non-dualism, or qualified non-dualism, or dualism based on the Upanishadic teachings, is denoted by this term.
Meaning or goal of the Vedas.
The oldest and the holiest of the Hindu scriptures, the primary source of authority in Hindu religion and philosophy. They are four in number: the Rig-veda, Sama-veda, Yajur-veda, and Atharva-Veda.
Of your relating to the Vedas.
Inquiry, analysis and reflection of the nature of the Self or truth.
Royal dynasty of Janaka; the kingdom of Mithila, native country of Sita.
Spiritual education, spiritual knowledge, learning, that which illumines, that which gives light, supreme teaching.
Highest wisdom; discriminating faculty of the intellect; spiritual wisdom beyond the material plane.
First incarnation of Brahma; Cosmic Divinity; Lord in His form as the physical manifested cosmos.
The Preserver, the Second of the Hindu Trinity of Brahma (the Creator), Vishnu (the Preserver), and Siva (the Destroyer).
Qualified nondualism. The doctrine that a person’s spirit has a qualified or partial identity with God.
Cosmic form, form of creation, name for the sun.
One of five vital airs; that which is diffused throughout the whole body.
Compiler of Vedas and author of the Mahabharatha, Mahabhagavatham, and Brahma Sutra.
Oblation, sacrifice, ceremony in which oblations are presented.
Holy ritual, sacrifice, or rite. Also, personification of rite (when capitalized).
Father of Nachiketas; a name for Gautama.
Great Upanishadic person. Priest and guru of King Janaka. Taught monistic (adwaithic)doctrine of identity of Atma and Brahman in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
Third and fourth sections of the Brihadaranyakopanishad, which deals with the spiritual teaching of Yajnavalkya to Janaka.
Second Veda, consisting of a collection of sacred texts in prose relating to sacrifices.

(a) Union of individual self or Atma with Supreme Being or Universal Self; act of yoking. (b) Spiritual discipline or exercise aimed at control of the senses. (c) Science of divine communion. (d) self control. Patanjali’s Yoga-sutras define yoga as a series of 8 steps leading to union with God.
Scripture or science that deals with yoga, esp. by Patanjali.
An aphoristic treatise on yoga by Patanjali.
Eldest Pandava brother; also called Dharmaraja.
Era or age. There is a cycle of four yugas: the Kritha yuga, Thretha yuga, Dwapara yuga, and Kali yuga. The present age is the Kali yuga.

gIntro: This glossary contains Sanskrit words, people, places, and literature that appear in Upanishad Vahini. Some Sanskrit words have made their way into English and appear in English dictionaries. A few of them are used without definition in the text, but they are defined in this glossary. Among them are Atma, dharma, guru, karma, yogas, and yogi. The text uses standard spellings for Sanskrit, and this glossary provides the same spellings. But some of the Sanskrit compounds have been hyphenated between their constituent words to aid those who want to analyze the meanings of individual words. When compound words are broken, individual words are given.
